title: Compound nouns and -daky
intro: Turkmen names many things by putting two nouns side by side: *türkmen halysy*, a Turkmen carpet; *awtobus duralgasy*, a bus stop. This unit shows how these compounds work and how endings go on them. Then come two endings that turn a word into a describer: `-dAky`, the one in a place (*öýdäki kitap*, the book at home), and `-ky` after the genitive, the one that belongs to someone (*meniňki*, mine).

sections.title: Bus stop, Turkmen carpet: noun compounds

blocks.text: To say what kind of thing something is, put a noun in front of another noun and give the second one the ending of **its**, `-(s)Y` ([A1 unit 9](a1-u09)): *awtobus*, bus, + *duralga*, stop → *awtobus duralgasy*, a bus stop. The first noun takes no ending at all. Word for word it is **bus, its stop**: the stop of the bus kind.

blocks.caption: Compounds you will see every day
head: Compound
Parts
Meaning

blocks.text: The second noun is the main one; the first narrows it down. Names of streets, towns and provinces work the same way: *Aşgabat şäheri*, the city of Ashgabat; *Mary welaýaty*, Mary province. Even *türkmen dili*, the Turkmen language, is a compound: *dil*, language, with **its**.

**Endings after a compound** go after `-(s)Y`, with the *n* that follows **its** ([A1 unit 10](a1-u10)): *awtobus duralgasynda*, at the bus stop; *Magtymguly köçesine*, to Magtymguly Street; *türkmen halysyny*, the Turkmen carpet, as an object. The plural comes before **its**: *mekdep sumkalary*, school bags.

items.en: I'm waiting at the bus stop.
The museum is on Magtymguly Street.
My mother bought the new Turkmen carpet.

blocks.title: Bare first, its second
blocks.text: The second noun needs **its**: *awtobus duralgasy*, not `awtobus duralga`. And the first noun stays bare: *towuk çorbasy*, chicken soup. With the genitive, *towugyň çorbasy*, it would be the soup of one particular chicken.

sections.title: My school bag, the centre of Ashgabat: possessives and the genitive

blocks.text: To say **my** school bag, swap **its** for **my**: *mekdep sumkasy* → *mekdep sumkam*. A word takes only one possessive, so `-(s)Y` gives way to the one you need, and the first noun still has no ending. The genitive pronoun can go in front, as with any possessive: *meniň mekdep sumkam*.

blocks.title: *mekdep sumkasy*: my school bag, your school bag…

blocks.text: **Compound or genitive?** A compound names a kind of thing, or a thing with a fixed name. When you mean one particular owner, or a part of one particular thing, put the first noun in the genitive instead, as in [A1 unit 10](a1-u10).

Meaning

blocks.text: A rule of thumb: if English could say it as one name for a kind of thing (**bus stop**, **school bag**, **phone number**), use the compound. If you mean **of** or **'s** about one particular thing or person, use the genitive. The two can meet: *Aýnanyň telefon nomeri*, Aýna's phone number.

items.en: There is a big museum in the centre of Ashgabat.

blocks.title: One possessive only
blocks.text: **My** replaces **its**: *mekdep sumkam*, not `mekdep sumkasym`. And **my** goes on the main noun, not the first one: not `mekdebim sumkasy`.

sections.title: The book at home, today's paper: -dAky and -ky

blocks.text: `-dAky` turns a place into a describing word: the locative `-dA`, where, plus `-ky`. *öýde*, at home → *öýdäki kitap*, the book (that is) at home. The new word goes before its noun, like an adjective: *Aşgabatdaky muzeý*, the museum in Ashgabat; *mekdepdäki mugallymlar*, the teachers at the school.

**Spelling.** Before *-ki* the *e* of `-de` becomes *ä*: *öýdäki*, *mekdepdäki*, *şäherdäki*. After back vowels it is *-daky*: *bazardaky*, *otagdaky*. A name keeps its capital, with no apostrophe: *Marydaky*, *Aşgabatdaky*. It is all one word.
It works after the place nouns of [A2 unit 9](a2-u09) too: *stoluň üstündäki telefon*, the phone on the table; *öýüň öňündäki maşyn*, the car in front of the house.

items.en: The books at home are old.
The museum in Ashgabat is very big.
The phone on the table is new.
My friend in Mary called me.

blocks.text: **`-ky` on time words.** Time words take `-ky` straight away, with no `-dA`: *şu gün*, today → *şu günki gazet*, today's paper; *düýn* → *düýnki sapak*, yesterday's lesson; *ertir* → *ertirki toý*, tomorrow's wedding; *gyş* → *gyşky eşik*, winter clothes. Two everyday words are made this way: *öňki*, previous, and *soňky*, last, latest: *soňky awtobus*, the last bus.

blocks.title: Where it is, or which one
blocks.text: *öýde* says where something is: *Kitap öýde*, the book is at home. *öýdäki* picks out a thing by its place: *öýdäki kitap*, the book at home. For **is at home**, the locative is enough: *Kitap öýde*, not `Kitap öýdäki`.

sections.title: Mine, yours, Aýna's: -ky after the genitive

blocks.text: Add `-ky` to a genitive and you get **the one belonging to**: *meniň*, my → *meniňki*, mine; *Aýnanyň*, Aýna's → *Aýnanyňky*, Aýna's (one). The word stands on its own, in place of a noun you don't need to repeat: *Bu kitap meniňki*, this book is mine.

blocks.title: *-ky* after the genitive pronouns: mine, yours…

blocks.text: Names and nouns work the same way: *Merdanyňky*, Merdan's; *kakamyňky*, my father's. Ask with *kimiňki?*, whose (one)?: *Bu telpek kimiňki?* — *Kakamyňky.* The question particle goes on the end: *Bu seniňkimi?*, is this yours?

items.en: Our house is big, theirs is small.

blocks.title: My and mine
blocks.text: English has two words, **my** and **mine**. Turkmen builds both on the same genitive: *meniň kitabym*, my book; *Kitap meniňki*, the book is mine.

blocks.title: Mine needs -ky
blocks.text: On its own, **mine** is *meniňki*: *Bu kitap meniňki*. The bare genitive *meniň* needs a noun after it: *meniň kitabym*.

summary: A compound names a kind of thing: the first noun bare, the second with **its**: *awtobus duralgasy*, *türkmen halysy*, *Magtymguly köçesi*.
Case endings follow **its**, with *n*: *duralgasynda*, *halysyny*; the plural comes before it: *mekdep sumkalary*.
With **my**, **your** and the rest, the possessive replaces **its**: *mekdep sumkam*, *telefon nomeriň*.
For one particular owner, use the genitive: *Aşgabadyň merkezi*, but *şäher merkezi*.
`-dAky` picks out a thing by its place: *öýdäki kitap*, *Aşgabatdaky muzeý*; the *e* becomes *ä* before *-ki*.
`-ky` after a genitive means **the one belonging to**: *meniňki*, *Aýnanyňky*, *kimiňki?*
